title: KV alloc stripes and compact mapper proposal
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a lightweight, runtime-friendly approach to reduce long-term fragmentation and improve eviction decisions in the KV cache by combining two complementary ideas: 1) allocation stripes (a low-overhead physical segregation to reduce cross-stream fragmentation) and 2) a compact-mapper layer that enables opportunistic relocation/compaction of small, live entries with minimal pause.

This is intentionally focused on the runtime side (no major on-disk format changes) and aims for an incremental rollout path that we can A/B behind a feature flag.

Background / motivation:

- Current allocator observations: workloads with mixed short/long sequence lengths produce many small entries (prefix cache) interleaved with large attention KV blobs. Over time these interleavings create internal fragmentation and increase the frequency and cost of large contiguous allocations.
- Eviction currently leans heavily on LRU-style heuristics and size buckets, but lacks a simple way to prefer evicting easily-relocatable objects vs objects that would cause fragmentation when freed.
- We need to reduce tail latencies for large allocation requests (model prompt spikes) without wholesale redesign of the runtime heap.

Goals:

- Reduce worst-case latency for large contiguous KV allocations by lowering fragmentation over medium horizons (minutes->hours).
- Keep runtime helpers single-threaded or lock-free where possible to avoid extra contention on hot allocation paths.
- Provide observability to reason about compaction cost vs latency benefit.
- Allow gradual opt-in per-cluster or per-machine; enable rollback to current allocator.

Constraints and assumptions:

- Target machines: GPU servers with large process heaps; allocation/deallocation rates are high and bursty during inference.
- We cannot introduce global stop-the-world compaction pauses longer than O(1ms) per compaction batch.
- Avoid requiring rewriting the entire KV encoding; compaction must be pointer-level relocation with stable lookup semantics.

Design overview (high-level):

1) Allocation stripes
   - Partition the heap address space used for KV cache into N stripes (N = small power-of-two, e.g., 4 or 8) per NUMA node. Each stripe is a collection of allocation arenas servicing a subset of logical allocation classes.
   - Stripe selection is based on fast hash of model_id + request_shard_id + sequence_length_bucket. The goal is to localize similar-lifetime objects in the same stripe to increase co-temporal free regions and reduce interleaving long/short lived objects.
   - Each stripe maintains its own free-lists and small-block sub-allocators. Cross-stripe allocations are allowed but discouraged; we prefer to satisfy a large contiguous allocation by scanning within the stripe first.

2) Compact-mapper layer
   - A thin indirection table maintained as part of the cache metadata: entry_id -> physical_ptr. This mapper is append-only for new allocations and can be updated atomically on relocation via CAS.
   - When a compaction relocation moves an object from old_ptr to new_ptr, the mapper is updated and the old memory is reclaimed. Callers always read through the mapper so relocation is transparent.
   - Mapper size: we expect O(#live_entries). Implement as sharded arrays keyed by entry handle (the handle is stable and small). The mapper lives in hot CPU memory and must be durable through restarts only for Private deployments (otherwise can be reconstructed on cache warm-start).

3) Eviction prioritization informed by relocation cost
   - Each cache entry carries a lightweight relocation_cost_score computed from: allocation_size, fragmentation_risk (a function of nearby hole sizes / stripe free-run profile), and recency/score from existing heuristics.
   - Eviction comparator is: prefer entries with low predicted relocation cost OR entries that when freed create large contiguous segments in the stripe.
   - For tie-breaking prefer higher LRU age.

Allocation flow (simplified):

- allocate(request):
  1) compute stripe = hash(model_id, shard, seq_bucket) % N
  2) try small-block allocator in stripe for size class S
  3) if not available, attempt to coalesce free runs within stripe (fast local compaction attempt)
  4) if still not available, consult compact-mapper: try relocation of a small number of low-relocation-cost entries to make a contiguous run big enough. This relocation is performed in-batch and bounded by relocated_bytes budget.
  5) if stripe-side fails, fallback to other stripes or global allocation as today.

Compaction mechanics and safety:

- Bounded relocations: every allocation that triggers compaction is allowed to relocate up to X KB (configurable) of live data. Default X is small (64KB) to limit pause impact.
- Relocations are performed by a dedicated background worker thread per NUMA node when possible; on-path allocations may perform a small synchronous relocation within the budget to avoid falling back to global allocator.
- Relocation steps:
  1) allocate target region (new_ptr) within same stripe (preferred)
  2) memcpy(src->dst) with write barrier to ensure GPU-visible memory consistency if needed (for mapped pinned memory)
  3) update compact-mapper entry via atomic CAS from old_ptr to new_ptr; if CAS fails, abort or re-read entry depending on policy
  4) reclaim old_ptr into stripe free-lists

- Consistency: callers access KV via the mapper handle; transient reads during relocation either see old_ptr or new_ptr depending on timing. We must ensure callers tolerate seeing stale-but-valid content for a short window (there is no destructive in-place update during relocation).

Fragmentation mitigation heuristics:

- Periodic compaction sweep per stripe triggered by fragmentation metrics: fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (largest_free_block / total_free_in_stripe). When fragmentation_ratio > threshold (e.g., 0.35) schedule background compaction targeting runs with many small free holes.
- Coalescing policy: maintain small-run deferred-coalesce to avoid frequent metadata churn; perform coalesces during low-load windows or when eviction budget permits.
- Superblocks: for very large allocations, maintain a superblock pool (contiguous pages reserved) to reduce allocation failures. Superblocks can be pre-allocated per stripe based on historical large-allocation frequency.

Observability and metrics to add:

- stripe_utilization_{stripe_id} (float)
- fragmentation_ratio_{stripe_id} (float)
- relocations/sec and relocated_bytes/sec (per-node)
- avg_relocation_latency_ms and p99_relocation_latency_ms
- reloc_failures (CAS conflict, out-of-space during relocation)
- large_alloc_failures_due_to_fragmentation
- eviction_relocation_score_histogram

Rollout plan / feature-flag strategy:

- Phase 0: feature flag off by default; metrics-only run (simulate mapper and stripe selection, compute predicted benefit but don’t relocate) for 2 weeks across canary pool.
- Phase 1: enable stripe allocation + mapper read-only (writes go to mapper but relocations disabled). Verify mapping cost and memory overhead.
- Phase 2: enable bounded on-path relocations with X = 64KB. Monitor reloc_latency and large_alloc_failures.
- Phase 3: increase budgets and enable background compaction sweeps; expose user-configurable stripe counts per-machine.

Open questions / risks:

- Mapper memory overhead: storing a 64-bit pointer per entry has non-trivial footprint. We need to estimate average live entries per machine and consider pointer compression (32-bit offset inside stripe) vs full pointer.
- CAS failure model under heavy concurrent reads/writes. Should we use versioned handles (handle + epoch) to make relocations idempotent?
- GPU pinned memory semantics: do we need explicit barriers after memcpy to ensure GPU sees updated KV? Different platforms (CUDA, ROCm) have subtle differences that we must account for in the memcpy+publish sequence.
- Edge cases in fallback allocation: if compaction fails repeatedly due to high churn we must avoid pathological CPU work—introduce backoff and fallthrough to global allocator quicker.

Bench / validation plan:

- Microbench: synthetic mix of short/long sequences to measure large_alloc_latency p50/p95/p99 with and without stripes+mapper.
- Production shadow: enable metrics-only mode on 10% of dedicated clusters to measure predicted fragmentation improvement and relocation load.
- Canary: enable full compact-mapper in one small region; set strict alerts on relocated_bytes/sec and p99 allocation latency increases.

Implementation notes and low-level APIs (sketch):

- new types: kv_handle (u64), compact_mapper_shard[] (atomic<uintptr_t>), stripe_arena struct with freelist headers and superblock list.
- APIs: mapper_get(handle) -> ptr, mapper_cas_update(handle, old_ptr, new_ptr) -> bool, stripe_try_relocate(stripe, budget) -> relocated_bytes.

Action items / next steps:

- [Marcus] prototype mapper as in-process shared vector, measure memory overhead for 8k/32k live-entry configs (due 2024-11-20).
- [Aisha] implement stripe allocator hook (striping + per-stripe freelists) and basic metrics (due 2024-12-05).
- [Diego] investigate GPU memory visibility semantics and propose safe memcpy+publish sequence (due 2024-11-15).
- [Lily] design observability dashboard mockups and alert thresholds (due 2024-11-29).

Notes to self / loose ideas:

- Could explore per-model stripe affinity (hot models get dedicated stripe) to further improve locality, but that increases configuration complexity.
- Consider a very lightweight relocation hint field in live entries to avoid touching large entries frequently (bump-on-write to deprioritize relocation).

References / links:

- Related internal docs: GH:serving-runtime allocator experiments (see linked artifacts).
- Prior notes: KV defrag observability playbook (use for alert thresholds).


This is an intentionally high-level design draft. Expect follow-ups with microbench results and a narrower implementation PR that focuses on the mapper memory layout and the very first fallback relocation case.
